query: For HfNbTaTiZr refractory high-entropy alloy, earlier studies separately examined tensile creep at 1250 °C, microhardness changes during cold rolling, elastic moduli from 293 to 1100 K, and hardening after aging at 600–800 °C. However, these findings do not provide a unified explanation of the alloy’s stress–strain and thermoelastic behavior. Thermal expansion is also relevant because mismatch can produce thermal stresses during composite solidification and potentially affect strength. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain the unresolved behavior? Specify a controlled comparison that would isolate the governing cause, observations predicted relative to a baseline, the relevant temperature and response boundaries, how the earlier findings support the hypothesis, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: The anomalous stress–strain and thermoelastic behavior of the HfNbTaTiZr RHEA is governed by an interplay between residual dislocation networks generated during cold rolling and local thermal stresses induced by differential thermal expansion. In this view, the lattice distortions from cold work—evidenced by dislocation bands—create a pre‐stressed microstructure that elevates the yield strength and enhances work hardening at lower to moderate temperatures. At elevated temperatures, however, thermal expansion mismatch across different grains (and potentially between composite phases if present) induces local stresses that reduce the activation barrier for dislocation motion, accelerating dynamic recovery or recrystallization. This combined effect explains the relatively small drop in tensile strength with temperature and the non‐monotonic changes in elastic moduli, as local internal stresses both stiffen and later promote softening depending on the temperature regime.
generation.material_initial_state: HfNbTaTiZr RHEA processed by cold rolling (with residual dislocation networks) versus a stress-relieved (annealed) counterpart exhibiting a relaxed, near-equilibrium dislocation density.
generation.intervention: Prepare two sets of samples: one set retained in the as-cold-rolled condition and another that is annealed to substantially reduce residual dislocation content. Then perform controlled tensile (and creep) tests and in situ elastic modulus measurements over a wide temperature range (from room temperature up to ~1250°C).
generation.conditions: Temperature varied from RT (~293 K) to high temperature (~1250°C or 1523 K); mechanical tests performed at constant strain rate and under conditions that allow for both elastic and plastic response to be measured; identical alloy chemical composition and microstructural scale, differing only by the level of residual dislocations.
generation.structural_mediator: Interactions between cold-work-induced residual dislocations and the local lattice distortions (including anisotropic thermal expansion mismatches) that generate internal thermo-mechanical stresses.
generation.mechanism: The residual dislocations from cold rolling produce local strain fields that harden the alloy at lower temperatures. With increasing temperature, these strain fields, coupled with inhomogeneous thermal expansion (which may vary between differently oriented grains or micro-regions), generate internal stresses that reduce the effective activation energy for dislocation glide, thus enhancing dynamic recovery or recrystallization. This competition between a high initial dislocation density (increasing yield and work hardening) and thermally induced stress relief leads to the observed modest strength reduction and peculiar thermoelastic response.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the annealed (stress-relieved) sample baseline, the as-cold-rolled sample should exhibit a more pronounced work-hardening effect and a higher yield strength at lower temperatures. However, at elevated temperatures (above ~800-900 K), the cold-worked sample will show an accelerated softening or a reduced stress level at equivalent strains due to enhanced dynamic recovery/recrystallization activated by the internally generated thermal stresses. Additionally, measurements of elastic moduli would reveal greater anisotropy (or unusual temperature evolution) in the cold-worked samples, reflecting the competing effects of residual stress and thermal expansion mismatch.
generation.baseline: The behavior of fully annealed, stress-relieved HfNbTaTiZr samples, which should show more conventional (monotonic) temperature dependencies in yield strength, work hardening, and elastic moduli.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is expected to hold in the temperature range from RT up to the creep regime (~1250°C), where both cold-work-induced residual stresses and thermally activated dislocation mobility are relevant. Deviations might occur if microstructural changes (e.g., phase transformations) occur outside this regime.
generation.uncertainty: This hypothesis builds on evidence of residual dislocation-induced work hardening from the cold rolled state (e.g., PMC10453588::web::013::3_results) combined with observations of unusual thermoelastic behavior and modest temperature dependence of elastic moduli (e.g., PMC11206460::web::018::elastic_isotropy_and_anisotropy_deformat). It extends these results by proposing that thermal expansion mismatch (a factor mentioned in the prompt) interacts with the residual stress state to modulate dislocation mobility. The exact quantitative interplay and the relative contributions of cold work versus thermal expansion mismatch remain to be determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HfNbTaTiZr samples: one in the as-cold-rolled state and one that is annealed to remove residual dislocations. Conduct identical tensile and creep tests over a temperature range from room temperature to ~1250°C. In situ measurements (e.g., neutron diffraction) should be used to evaluate elastic moduli and lattice strains during deformation.
measurements: Yield strength and work-hardening rates at various temperatures
Creep rate under a constant load at elevated temperatures
Lattice strain evolution and elastic moduli via in situ neutron diffraction
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the removal of residual dislocations by annealing does not significantly alter the temperature dependence of the yield strength, work hardening, creep behavior, and elastic modulus evolution (i.e., if both cold-worked and annealed samples show similar responses without evidence of additional thermal stress effects), then the hypothesis that the combined influences of residual dislocations and thermal expansion mismatch govern the observed behavior would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The differentials between the UTS and YS were about 100 MPa, and gradually widened as the temperature rose. Work hardening appeared in all curves from RT to 1073 K. We speculated that this was due to the fact that the heat treatment did not completely eliminate the residual stress of the alloy after cold rolling [,]. In order to prove this, the rolled samples were analyzed by transmission electron microscopy before a tensile test (see Figure 5). Some obvious dense dislocation bands were found in Figure 5a, and in addition, the diffraction pattern indicated that the alloy retained the structure of a single-phase BCC after the prior treatment. The region where the dislocation band was located was enlarged to further analyze its composition. In Figure 5b, it can be clearly found that the previously thought dislocation band was composed of two rows of dislocations. After a further enlargement, it was found that each dislocation band was composed of dense, short dislocations. This proved the previous conjecture that the residual dislocation after cold rolling caused a work hardening of the alloy.

cited_evidence.text: Typically, the response of lattice strains under applied stresses is strongly associated with the oriented grains due to the effects of elastic anisotropies in polycrystalline metal materials (, ), including FCC-structured HEAs (). The elastically anisotropic deformations originate from the orientation-dependent elastic modulus, which is presented by the different slopes in the plots of the lattice strain evolution as a function of applied stresses. In the case of BCC-structured materials, the {110} and {211} grains, which have higher elastic stiffness than other grains, exhibit the larger slopes. The {200} and {310} grains, on the other hand, have smaller slopes with lower elastic stiffness (, ). After this elastic stretch, the sequence of grain yielding depends on the value of the Schmid factor, showing varying stress levels for the onset of yielding in differently grains, which is commonly characterized as the grain-to-grain yielding behaviors (). The plastic anisotropy is derived from the occurrence of plastic deformation on certain (hkl) grains, on which slip is preferred to occur.
